title: the half-golden mongoose
hookLine: the great sacrifice is finished and praised by all, and a mongoose with half a golden body says it isn't worth a handful of flour
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
tomorrow: the Pandavas walk out of the city for the last time. what do they leave behind?

cards: Gold handed out to the brahmanas, food for everyone, kings and sages crowding the grounds: the horse is home, the sacrifice is done, and everyone says there's never been a rite like it.
Then, from a hole in the ground, out comes a mongoose. One side of its body is gold.

It looks around at all this splendor and speaks, in a voice like thunder: this sacrifice of yours isn't equal to a little barley flour given away by a poor brahmana in Kurukshetra. The crowd goes silent.

teach.b: In Kurukshetra, the mongoose explains, there lived a brahmana who fed his family by gleaning, picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest. A famine came, and the family went hungry for a long time.
At last he gathered enough barley for a little flour, and they divided it four ways: the man, his wife, their son and the son's wife. Just as they were about to eat, a hungry guest arrived.
The brahmana welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers.
Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. Then the guest revealed himself: he was Dharma, righteousness itself, and the family was carried to heaven.
The mongoose had rolled in the scattered flour, and wherever it touched, its fur turned to gold. Half of it. Ever since, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, hoping to turn the other half gold.
It just rolled in Yudhishthira's. Nothing changed. Here's the teaching.
The Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student going home: let your guest be a god to you, atithi devo bhava.
That's why Hindu families feed the guest first, and in this story the guest really was Dharma.
And in the Gita, Krishna asks only a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD
teach.b: A gift is weighed by what it cost and the love in it, not by its size.

how: The story of the mongoose and the gleaner's flour closes the account of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice in the Ashvamedhika Parva; storytellers retell it to teach that a gift given in want outweighs great display, and that the guest is to be honored as God.

o: a feast held when a royal rite is done
the book of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice
a golden prize given to the bravest king

games.q: the mongoose's story — tap the pairs.
p: one side of its body gold
gave every share of flour away
turned none of the fur gold

s: in Hindu teaching, a bigger gift always counts for more
the gleaner's flour outweighed a king's sacrifice; the Gita asks only a leaf or a flower, given with love.
the family gave their food while they were starving
it was a famine, and each gave their own share.
rolling in Yudhishthira's sacrifice turned the mongoose fully gold
nothing changed; it's still half gold.

games.q: an unexpected guest arrives right at dinner, and there's barely enough. by the gleaner's family, what fits?
o: serve the guest first: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God.
eat first, then offer what's left.
say you've already eaten so they'll go home.
games.why: the gleaner's family gave every share to the guest, and the guest was Dharma. that's why Hindu families feed the guest first.

practice: Rest your hands palms up in your lap, as if holding a small bowl. Many Hindu families set aside the first portion of a meal before anyone eats, for a guest, a cow, or anyone hungry.
Think of your last meal, and of who else might have been hungry at that hour.
Then think of one small portion, not grand, just real, that you could set aside; if you pray, offer that intention in your prayer, and if you don't, simply decide it.

wordCard.voice: Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which ends with a mongoose weighing it against a poor family's flour.

orig.note: nakula: a mongoose; the same word is the name of one of the Pandava twins.

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. A handful of barley outweighed a king's gold. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, the mongoose at Yudhishthira's sacrifice and the story of the gleaning brahmana of Kurukshetra and his gift of barley flour
